claims.claim: Aggressive gestures in BMRs include strong strikes and opponent-pushing with the head, open mouth sniffing and biting.
claims.source: Other aggressive gestures include strong strikes and opponent-pushing with the head, open mouth sniffing (exposed incisors; Figure 4) and biting (Nevo et al., 1986).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nevo et al., 1986 and references Figure 4.

claims.claim: Aggressive behaviors in BMRs increase where there is more competition for resource availability.
claims.source: These behaviors were shown to increase where there is more competition for resource availability (Nevo et al., 1982).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nevo et al., 1982.

claims.claim: Female BMRs present lower aggression intensity compared to males.
claims.source: Females were reported to present lower aggression intensity compared to males (Nevo et al., 1986)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nevo et al., 1986.

claims.claim: The behavioral component of aggressive behaviors in BMRs is independent of testosterone levels in males.
claims.source: nevertheless, the behavioral component of these behaviors was shown to be independent of testosterone levels in male BMRs (Gottreich et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gottreich et al., 2001.

claims.claim: BMRs engage in head drumming 'duets' back and forth across territories.
claims.source: It has been noted that BMRs engage in head drumming 'duets' back and forth across territories (Rado et al., 1987)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rado et al., 1987.

claims.claim: The types of information encoded in BMR head drumming signals are not well understood.
claims.source: but the types of information encoded in the signal (for example the signaler's level of dominance, sex, age, or individual identity) are not well understood (Randall, 2013; Seyfarth and Cheney, 2003; Tibbetts and Dale, 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations indicating the lack of understanding.

claims.claim: Courtship in BMRs involves multimodal signaling including seismic head drums, vocal 'purrs' and olfactory cues, and engaging in tactile behaviors.
claims.source: At a close distance to the female's tunnel, courtship ensues, involving multimodal signaling including seismic head drums, vocal 'purrs' and olfactory cues, and engaging in tactile behaviors until the female decides to mate with the male (Gazit and Terkel, 2000; Nevo, 1961; Nevo, 1969; Shanas et al., 1995; Figures 2 and 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations and references to Figures 2 and 4.

claims.claim: Copulatory pairs of BMRs spend brief periods together, retreating to their individual territories after mating.
claims.source: Copulatory pairs spend brief periods together, retreating to their individual territories after mating (Gazit and Terkel, 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gazit and Terkel, 2000.

claims.claim: Estrous female BMRs are able to discriminate chromosomal subspecies of male BMRs by their courtship calls.
claims.source: It was observed that estrous females are able to discriminate chromosomal subspecies of male BMRs by their courtship calls, and that in most cases, estrous females would prefer the calls of their homospecific mates over those of heterospecific ones (Nevo et al., 1987).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nevo et al., 1987.

claims.claim: Gestation period in BMRs is 34 days.
claims.source: Gestation period in BMRs is 34 days, after which the female delivers a litter of 3–4 pups on average (Gazit et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gazit et al., 1996.

claims.claim: Female BMRs deliver a litter of 3–4 pups on average.
claims.source: Gestation period in BMRs is 34 days, after which the female delivers a litter of 3–4 pups on average (Gazit et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gazit et al., 1996.

claims.claim: Mother and pups in BMRs communicate by vocalizations in the first stages of ontogeny, and gradually shift to seismic communication of head drumming duets.
claims.source: Mother and pups communicate by vocalizations in the first stages of ontogeny, and gradually shift to seismic communication of head drumming duets (Rado et al., 1991b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rado et al., 1991b.

claims.claim: Mother BMRs show higher communication and aggression toward male pups compared to female pups prior to complete dispersal.
claims.source: Interestingly, Gazit and Terkel, 1998 reported sex differences in mother-pup interactions prior to a complete dispersal, as mother's communication and aggression toward male pups was longer and more frequent compared to those toward female pups.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gazit and Terkel, 1998.

claims.claim: Dispersal of juvenile BMRs starts approximately 2 months after parturition.
claims.source: This process leads to the gradual dispersal of the juveniles, starting approximately 2 months after parturition (Gazit and Terkel, 1998)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gazit and Terkel, 1998.

claims.claim: Juvenile BMRs establish their own solitary territories at the age of approximately 3 months.
claims.source: and ending in the individual establishment of their own solitary territories at the age of approximately 3 months (Rado et al., 1991b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rado et al., 1991b.

claims.claim: BMRs integrate photoperiodic changes and entrain a circadian activity rhythm by light received through their atrophied eyes.
claims.source: Despite residing almost exclusively underground, BMRs were shown to integrate photoperiodic changes and entrain a circadian activity rhythm by light received through their atrophied eyes (see section 'Circadian rhythm')
claims.evidence: This claim references another section of the manuscript for supporting evidence.

claims.claim: In male prairie voles, alteration of both temperature and photoperiod caused regression in synthesis of gonadotropin-releasing hormone and in their reproductive function.
claims.source: In male prairie voles (Microtus ochrogaster), alteration of both temperature and photoperiod caused regression in synthesis of gonadotropin-releasing hormone, and in their reproductive function (Kriegsfeld et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kriegsfeld et al., 2001.

claims.claim: BMRs are generalists that forage and cache encountered food items, such as geophytes and herbaceous plants.
claims.source: BMRs are generalists that forage and cache encountered food items, such as geophytes and herbaceous plants (Galil, 1967; Heth, 1989, Lövy et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: BMR foraging and food-caching behaviors are essential to ensure survival throughout the year.
claims.source: The BMR's foraging and food-caching behaviors are essential to ensure survival throughout the year (Rado et al., 1993; Vleck, 1979).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rado et al., 1993 and Vleck, 1979.

claims.claim: In the summer, BMRs stay largely inactive in tunnels at deeper and cooler depths (>40 cm).
claims.source: In the summer, individuals stay largely inactive in tunnels at deeper and cooler depths (>40 cm) (Rado et al., 1993)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rado et al., 1993.

claims.claim: BMRs have far superior spatial memories compared to rats, learning a maze significantly faster.
claims.source: BMRs were shown to have far superior spatial memories compared to rats, learning a maze significantly faster, and retaining 45% of their performance 120 days later (Kimchi and Terkel, 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimchi and Terkel, 2001.

claims.claim: BMRs retain 45% of their maze performance 120 days later.
claims.source: BMRs were shown to have far superior spatial memories compared to rats, learning a maze significantly faster, and retaining 45% of their performance 120 days later (Kimchi and Terkel, 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimchi and Terkel, 2001.

claims.claim: BMR tunnels can be as long as 100 m.
claims.source: While it is unclear how many food caches BMRs may have branching off their tunnels, which can be as long as 100 m
claims.evidence: This is stated as a fact about BMR tunnel length.

claims.claim: BMRs possess rudimentary eyes less than 1 mm in diameter that are covered by furred skin.
claims.source: While blind mole rats appear as if they have no eyes, they do possess rudimentary eyes (less than 1 mm in diameter), that are covered by furred skin (Cooper et al., 1993b, Haim et al., 1983; ; Rado et al., 1992; Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations and references Figure 2.

claims.claim: The lens of the BMR is degenerated and embedded within a hypertrophied harderian gland.
claims.source: The lens of the BMR is degenerated and embedded within a hypertrophied harderian gland (Cooper et al., 1993b, Haim et al., 1983; Rado et al., 1992).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: The BMR's retina contains < 900 ganglion cells.
claims.source: The BMR's retina contains < 900 ganglion cells (Cooper et al., 1993a)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cooper et al., 1993a.

claims.claim: Rat retinas contain >50,000 ganglion cells.
claims.source: a significantly low number compared to >50,000 cells found in rats, for example (Gao et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gao et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Brain structures involved in image processing are severely regressed and dysfunctional in the BMR.
claims.source: Moreover, brain structures involved in image processing are severely regressed and dysfunctional in the BMR (Cooper et al., 1993a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cooper et al., 1993a.

claims.claim: The dorsal lateral geniculate body in BMRs is strongly activated by auditory stimuli.
claims.source: For instance, the dorsal lateral geniculate body, which is the primary visual nuclei in the thalamus of sighted mammals, that sends visual information to the visual cortex, was reported to be strongly activated by auditory stimuli in BMRs (Bronchti et al., 2002; Bronchti et al., 1989; Heil et al., 1991).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: The BMR's retina lacks short-wave opsine cones.
claims.source: Although the BMR's retina lacks short-wave opsine cones (David-Gray et al., 2002)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to David-Gray et al., 2002.

claims.claim: The BMR's retina includes at least three types of photoreceptors (rodopsin, coneopsin and L/M cone opsin).
claims.source: it includes at least three types of photoreceptors (rodopsin, coneopsin and L/M cone opsin) that collect the scant light penetrating the soil (Burda, 2006; David-Gray et al., 1999; Esquiva et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Light induces gene expression in the BMR's suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN).
claims.source: Therefore, despite being blind, light induces gene expression in the SCN (Vuillez et al., 1994)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vuillez et al., 1994.

claims.claim: Light entrains circadian rhythms of locomotor behavior in the BMR.
claims.source: and entrains circadian rhythms of locomotor behavior in the BMR (David-Gray et al., 1998; Rado et al., 1991a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to David-Gray et al., 1998 and Rado et al., 1991a.

claims.claim: Enucleation abolished light-induced reactions in BMRs.
claims.source: These reactions to light rely upon retinal photoreceptors, since enucleation abolished them (David-Gray et al., 1998; Pevet et al., 1984; Rado et al., 1991a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: The BMR's harderian gland is able to synthesize melatonin.
claims.source: In addition to the atrophied eyes, the BMR's harderian gland is also involved in photoperiodic perception, as it is able to synthesize melatonin (Balemans et al., 1980)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Balemans et al., 1980.

claims.claim: The BMR's harderian gland is involved in photoperiodic detection.
claims.source: and it was shown to be involved in photoperiodic detection (Pevet et al., 1984).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pevet et al., 1984.

claims.claim: Melatonin receptors were found in the BMR's harderian gland.
claims.source: Melatonin receptors were also found in the BMR's harderian gland, and were suggested to take part in a negative feedback control of melatonin production (Gilad et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gilad et al., 1997.

claims.claim: The eusocial, subterranean Damaraland mole-rat possesses a circadian melatonin rhythm that is modulated according to photoperiodic changes.
claims.source: Interestingly, the eusocial, subterranean Damaraland mole-rat was also shown to possess a circadian melatonin rhythm that is modulated according to photoperiodic changes (Richter et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Richter et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Blind mole rats have magnetoreception abilities.
claims.source: Kimchi and Terkel, 2001 demonstrated that blind mole rats have magnetoreception abilities, and that they rely on them when choosing the locations for their nests and food caches.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimchi and Terkel, 2001.

claims.claim: When shifting the polarity of the earth's magnetic field by 180̊, BMRs shifted the location of their preferred nest and food cache sites accordingly.
claims.source: When shifting the polarity of the earth's magnetic field by 180̊, BMRs shifted the location of their preferred nest and food cache sites accordingly (Kimchi and Terkel, 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimchi and Terkel, 2001.

claims.claim: Following surgical removal of their eyes, individual Ansell's mole-rat demonstrated impaired magnetic sensing.
claims.source: In addition, following surgical removal of their eyes, individual Ansell's mole-rat (Fukomys anselli) demonstrated impaired magnetic sensing, supporting the hypothesis that in mole rats, magnetoreception receptors are located in the cornea (Caspar et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Caspar et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Experiments on BMR magnetoreception were conducted in total darkness.
claims.source: However, some observations in BMRs suggest that the their magnetoreception is independent of light, as experiments were conducted in total darkness (Kimchi and Terkel, 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimchi and Terkel, 2001.

claims.claim: The Zambian mole rat's perception of the earth's magnetic field is independent of light.
claims.source: This finding is supported by a study of another mole rat species, the Zambian mole rat (Fukomys amatus), that was shown to be independent of light in its perception of the earth's magnetic field (Marhold et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Marhold et al., 1997.

claims.claim: Fossorial and subterranean animals generally hear better at low frequencies and have restricted hearing ranges, compared to surface-dwelling rodents.
claims.source: Accordingly, fossorial and subterranean animals generally hear better at low frequencies and have restricted hearing ranges, compared to surface-dwelling rodents that have been known to produce frequencies as high as in the ultrasonic range (Dent et al., 2018; He et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dent et al., 2018 and He et al., 2021.

claims.claim: The Highveld mole rat is more sensitive to very low frequencies (0.8 kHz).
claims.source: The Highveld mole rat (Müller and Burda, 1989) and the Zambian mole rat (Brückmann and Burda, 1997), both subterranean rodents, are more sensitive to very low frequencies (0.8 kHz)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Müller and Burda, 1989.

claims.claim: The Zambian mole rat is more sensitive to very low frequencies (0.8 kHz).
claims.source: The Highveld mole rat (Müller and Burda, 1989) and the Zambian mole rat (Brückmann and Burda, 1997), both subterranean rodents, are more sensitive to very low frequencies (0.8 kHz)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brückmann and Burda, 1997.

claims.claim: The surface-dwelling feral house mouse is most sensitive to higher frequencies (16 kHz).
claims.source: while the surface-dwelling feral house mouse (Heffner and Masterton, 1980) is most sensitive to higher frequencies (16 kHz).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Heffner and Masterton, 1980.

claims.claim: Peak sensitivity in the surface-dwelling guinea pig is –9 dB SPL.
claims.source: For example, peak sensitivity in the surface-dwelling guinea pig (Cavia porcellus) is –9 dB SPL (sound pressure level) (Prosen et al., 1978)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Prosen et al., 1978.

claims.claim: Peak sensitivity in the subterranean naked mole rat is 35 dB SPL.
claims.source: while in the subterranean naked mole rat it is just 35 dB SPL (Heffner and Heffner, 1993).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Heffner and Heffner, 1993.

claims.claim: Trained blind mole rats can hear between 54 Hz and 5.6 kHz at an amplitude of 60 dB SPL.
claims.source: Results from behavioral audiograms showed that trained blind mole rats can hear between 54 Hz and 5.6 kHz at an amplitute of 60 dB SPL , with peak sensitivity at 1 kHz at 32 dB SPL (Heffner and Heffner, 1992).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Heffner and Heffner, 1992.

claims.claim: Blind mole rats have peak hearing sensitivity at 1 kHz at 32 dB SPL.
claims.source: Results from behavioral audiograms showed that trained blind mole rats can hear between 54 Hz and 5.6 kHz at an amplitute of 60 dB SPL , with peak sensitivity at 1 kHz at 32 dB SPL (Heffner and Heffner, 1992).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Heffner and Heffner, 1992.

claims.claim: Blind mole rats have poor sound localization abilities.
claims.source: Additionally, blind mole rats have poor sound localization abilities, as demonstrated from playback of left and right speakers with 180o of separation (Heffner and Heffner, 1992).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Heffner and Heffner, 1992.

claims.claim: Blind mole rats cannot localize signals less than 400 ms in duration.
claims.source: Blind mole rats cannot localize signals less than 400 ms in duration, and performed best at localizing sound bursts of 1.2ms (Heffner and Heffner, 1992).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Heffner and Heffner, 1992.

claims.claim: Blind mole rats performed best at localizing sound bursts of 1.2 ms.
claims.source: Blind mole rats cannot localize signals less than 400 ms in duration, and performed best at localizing sound bursts of 1.2ms (Heffner and Heffner, 1992).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Heffner and Heffner, 1992.

claims.claim: The BMR lacks an external pinna of the outer ear.
claims.source: The lower hearing sensitivity and minimal localization ability are apparent in the morphology of the BMR, which lacks an external pinna of the outer ear (see ear opening location in Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This claim references Figure 2 for visual evidence.

claims.claim: The BMR's middle and inner ear are uniquely structured, creating inefficient transmission of airborne sound.
claims.source: The BMR's middle and inner ear are uniquely structured, creating inefficient transmission of airborne sound (Rado et al., 1989).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rado et al., 1989.

claims.claim: Giant mole rats have a repertoire of 14 call types as determined by behavioral context and spectro-temporal features.
claims.source: Giant mole rats (Fukomys mechowii) were demonstrated to have a repertoire of 14 call types as determined by behavioral context, such as teeth-fencing and predator alarm, and by spectro-temporal features (Bednářová et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bednářová et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Giant mole rat calls have peak frequencies of less than 5 kHz.
claims.source: In accordance with their low frequency hearing ranges, these calls are low in frequency, with peak frequencies of less than 5 kHz (Bednářová et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bednářová et al., 2013.

claims.claim: The eusocial naked mole rat has dialects in the 'soft chirp' call type across colonies that signifies group membership.
claims.source: The eusocial naked mole rat was recently shown to have dialects in the 'soft chirp' call type across colonies that signifies group membership (Barker et al., 2021b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Barker et al., 2021b.

claims.claim: At least six call types determined by behavioral context, all with frequencies below 8 kHz, have been noted in BMRs.
claims.source: At least six call types determined by behavioral context, all with frequencies below 8 kHz, have been noted thus far (Capranica et al., 1974).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Capranica et al., 1974.

claims.claim: Different call types in BMRs are used to facilitate mother and pup communication.
claims.source: Different call types are used to facilitate mother and pup communication (Capranica et al., 1974; Gazit and Terkel, 1998; Rado et al., 1991b)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Different call types in BMRs are used in male courtship displays during the mating season.
claims.source: and used in male courtship displays during the mating season (Gazit and Terkel, 2000; Nevo, 1969).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gazit and Terkel, 2000 and Nevo, 1969.

claims.claim: BMR courtship calls differ in frequency and temporal components across the Spalax chromosomal subspecies.
claims.source: These courtship calls differ in frequency and temporal components across the Spalax chromosomal subspecies, and appear to play a role in assortative mating between the neighboring populations (Heth et al., 1988; Nevo et al., 1987)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Heth et al., 1988 and Nevo et al., 1987.

claims.claim: Distress calls in BMRs have peak frequencies between 4 and 6 kHz.
claims.source: Distress calls with peak frequencies between 4 and 6 kHz have also been opportunistically observed in lab studies (Bronchti et al., 1989).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bronchti et al., 1989.

claims.claim: A BMR produces vibrational signals by drumming on the ceiling of its tunnel with the large, flattened portion of its head, producing bursts of head drums (approx. 2–4 drums per burst, 0.3 s duration).
claims.source: A BMR produces vibrational signals by drumming on the ceiling of its tunnel with the large, flattened portion of its head, producing bursts of head drums (approx. 2–4 drums per burst, 0.3 s duration) (Heth et al., 1987; Rado et al., 1987; Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Heth et al., 1987 and Rado et al., 1987, and references Figure 4.

claims.claim: BMR seismic signals range in the frequency of approximately 100–250 Hz and may travel as far as 10 m or more.
claims.source: Seismic signals range in the frequency of approximately 100–250 Hz and may travel as far as 10 m or more (Heth et al., 1987; Rado et al., 1987).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Heth et al., 1987 and Rado et al., 1987.

claims.claim: BMRs perceive seismic signals by pressing the side of their lower jaw against the tunnel wall, which transmits the signals to the inner ear by means of bone conduction.
claims.source: Perception of seismic signals is achieved in two ways, one by pressing the side of their lower jaw against the tunnel wall, which transmits the signals to the inner ear by means of bone conduction (Mason et al., 2010; Rado et al., 1989; Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mason et al., 2010 and Rado et al., 1989, and references Figure 4A.

claims.claim: BMRs perceive seismic signals via mechanoreceptors located on their paws.
claims.source: The Second is via mechanoreceptors located on their paws (Kimchi et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimchi et al., 2005.

claims.claim: Providing a vibration stimulus in contact with the lower jaw evoked responses in the auditory brainstem of BMRs.
claims.source: Providing a vibration stimulus in contact with the lower jaw evoked responses in the auditory brainstem, and bilaterally deafened mole rats, showed loss of response and eventual ceasing of head drumming behavior in the course of 4–6 weeks (Rado et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rado et al., 1998.

claims.claim: Bilaterally deafened BMRs showed loss of response to vibration stimuli and eventual ceasing of head drumming behavior in the course of 4–6 weeks.
claims.source: Providing a vibration stimulus in contact with the lower jaw evoked responses in the auditory brainstem, and bilaterally deafened mole rats, showed loss of response and eventual ceasing of head drumming behavior in the course of 4–6 weeks (Rado et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rado et al., 1998.

claims.claim: The occipital cortex in BMRs is activated by frequencies corresponding to both vibrational and acoustic signals.
claims.source: Furthermore, the occipital cortex, usually associated with vision, was shown to be activated by frequencies corresponding to both vibrational and acoustic signals (Bronchti et al., 2002; Heil et al., 1991; Sadka and Wollberg, 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Two clusters of cells in the BMR cortex fired in response to frequencies centered around 2.5–4.4 kHz, matching airborne social vocalizations, and to 100 Hz, matching the frequency of long-distance vibratory signals.
claims.source: Specifically, two clusters of cells fired in response to frequencies centered around 2.5–4.4 kHz, matching airborne social vocalizations, and to 100 Hz, matching the frequency of long-distance vibratory signals (Sadka and Wollberg, 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sadka and Wollberg, 2004.

claims.claim: The BMR's somatosensory cortex extends far into the occipital cortex.
claims.source: In addition to the auditory cortex, it was further shown that the BMR's somatosensory cortex also extends far into the occipital cortex (Necker et al., 1992; Rehkämper et al., 1994).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Necker et al., 1992 and Rehkämper et al., 1994.

claims.claim: The somatosensory system in the isocortex of the blind mole rat is 1.7 times larger compared to the laboratory rat, when taking into consideration the differences in body weight and brain size.
claims.source: The somatosensory system in the isocortex of the blind mole rat was shown to be 1.7 times larger compared to the laboratory rat, when taking into consideration the differences in body weight and brain size of the two species (Mann et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mann et al., 1997.

claims.claim: The dermal papillae of the rhinarium in the BMR contains a few Merkel cell-axon complexes and simple Meissner's corpuscles.
claims.source: Klauer and colleagues found that the dermal papillae of the rhinarium in the BMR contains a few Merkel cell-axon complexes and simple Meissner's corpuscles.
claims.evidence: This claim is attributed to Klauer and colleagues in the text.

claims.claim: BMRs consistently engage in a 'wall seeking' behavior during maze learning and exploration tasks.
claims.source: During maze learning and exploration tasks, BMRs consistently engage in a 'wall seeking' behavior, in which they press their bodies against the side of the wall, sometimes alternating sides, and brushing the vibrissae against the maze surfaces (Kimchi et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimchi et al., 2004.

claims.claim: Blind mole rats performed significantly better in a narrow maze which allowed constant contact with the wall, compared to a maze twice the width of their body diameter.
claims.source: When comparing maze learning and performance, blind mole rats performed significantly better in a narrow maze which allowed constant contact with the wall, compared to a maze twice the width of their body diameter (Kimchi and Terkel, 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimchi and Terkel, 2000.

claims.claim: Rats performed better in the wider maze compared to the narrow maze.
claims.source: In contrast, rats performed better in the wider maze (Kimchi et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimchi et al., 2004.

claims.claim: BMRs dig their tunnels to exactly the diameter of their own body width.
claims.source: In nature, BMRs dig their tunnels to exactly the diameter of their own body width, in order to obtain maximal tactile information (Kimchi and Terkel, 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimchi and Terkel, 2002.

claims.claim: For naked mole rats, the incisors are represented in approximately 31% of the somatosensory cortex.
claims.source: Additionally, for naked mole rats which use their teeth for digging, foraging, social encounters, and moving pups, the incisors are represented in approximately 31% of the somatosensory cortex (Catania and Remple, 2002; Park et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Catania and Remple, 2002 and Park et al., 2007.

claims.claim: BMRs use seismic signaling as an echolocation behavior.
claims.source: Kimchi and colleagues demonstrated that BMRs use seismic signaling as an echolocation behavior (Kimchi et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimchi et al., 2005.

claims.claim: In field experiments, blind mole rats were able to detect obstacles placed by researchers in their tunnels and repeatedly dug around or over them.
claims.source: In field experiments, blind mole rats were able to detect obstacles placed by the researchers in their tunnels (various size ditches), and repeatedly dug around or over them.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from field experiments.

claims.claim: The bypass strategy of BMRs varied depending on the size of the obstacle.
claims.source: The bypass strategy varied depending on the size of the obstacle (large/small ditches), likely to minimize energetic costs (Kimchi and Terkel, 2003a, Kimchi and Terkel, 2003b; Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kimchi and Terkel, 2003a and 2003b, and references Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Head drums used for echolocation in BMRs are higher in frequency (250–300 Hz) and produced as a single hit rather than bursts at intervals of approximately 8 s.
claims.source: Unlike head drums used for intraspecific communication, these drums were higher in frequency (250–300 Hz) and produced as a single hit rather than bursts at intervals of approximately 8 s (Kimchi et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimchi et al., 2005.

claims.claim: The amplitude and frequency of the wavelengths recorded by geophones are sufficient for rapid detection of reflected waves when the BMR is 30–50 cm away from an obstacle.
claims.source: Through modeling, it was demonstrated that the amplitude and frequency of the wavelengths recorded by geophones are sufficient for rapid detection of reflected waves when the individual is 30–50 cm away from an obstacle (Kimchi et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimchi et al., 2005.

claims.source: Being congenitally blind, Spalax ehrenbergi is deprived of visual inputs, and thus compensates via the diversion of the visual modality to the auditory modality.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fang et al., 2014 and Malik et al., 2011.

claims.source: and scRNA sequencing of microglia revealed similarities of BMRs to other rodents (Geirsdottir et al., 2019).

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hadi, 2020a and Hadi et al., 2020b.

results.result: The blind mole rat (BMR) is an exceedingly solitary, territorial, and aggressive subterranean rodent that possesses specialized sensory systems for social communication and navigation in underground tunnels.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 are well-supported by extensive citations throughout the manuscript describing BMR behavioral characteristics and sensory adaptations. The manuscript provides detailed evidence from multiple studies documenting solitary behavior (C16, C17), territorial aggression (C18-C22), and specialized sensory systems including vibrational communication (C83-C90), auditory adaptations (C68-C74), and somatosensory specializations (C91-C97).

results.result: Social isolation produces negative physiological and behavioral effects in social rodent species, including cardiovascular dysfunction and depression in prairie voles and impaired GABAergic function with increased aggression in mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C4 and C5 are supported by specific citations (McNeal et al., 2014; Matsumoto et al., 2005) and serve to establish the contrast between social species that suffer from isolation and solitary species like the BMR that have evolved for solitary living.

results.result: Among subterranean rodents, 14 of 19 known genera are solitary, while only two species (naked mole-rat and Damaraland mole-rat) are eusocial mammals.
results.evaluation: Claims C6 and C7 are supported by citations (Nevo, 1979; Bennett and Jarvis, 1988; Barker et al., 2021a) and establish the phylogenetic context for understanding the BMR's position on the social behavior spectrum among subterranean rodents.

results.result: BMRs weigh 100-250g, inhabit various Middle Eastern habitats, exhibit high longevity (20+ years), and demonstrate cancer resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C11 are supported by multiple citations providing basic biological characteristics of BMRs. These descriptive claims establish the BMR as a unique model organism with exceptional physiological properties.

results.result: Mice and rats are highly social animals and therefore unsuitable for studying naturally-occurring anti-social and solitary behaviors.
results.evaluation: Claim C12 is supported by citation (Ellenbroek and Youn, 2016), and C13 follows logically as an inference. This establishes the rationale for using BMR as an alternative model organism for studying anti-social behaviors.

results.result: Humans with autism spectrum disorders, antisocial personality disorders, depression, or Alzheimer's disease often present decreased socialization and increased aggressiveness.
results.evaluation: Claim C14 is supported by multiple citations and establishes the translational relevance of studying BMR behavior for understanding human psychiatric conditions with social deficits.

results.result: BMRs are seasonal breeders that live solitarily year-round except for brief winter mating periods, with territorial encounters causing extreme stress and aggression often resulting in death.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C17 are well-supported by multiple citations (Shanas et al., 1995; Nevo, 1961; Rado et al., 1993; Zuri et al., 1998b) describing the BMR's reproductive seasonality and extreme territorial aggression.

results.result: BMR aggressive behaviors include retreat-and-attack postures, bulldozing, head strikes, biting, and open-mouth sniffing, with behaviors increasing under resource competition; females show lower aggression intensity than males, but aggression is independent of testosterone levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C22 are supported by multiple citations (Guttman et al., 1975; Nevo et al., 1986, 1982; Gottreich et al., 2001) providing detailed descriptions of aggressive behaviors and their modulation. The testosterone-independence finding (C22) is particularly notable.

results.result: BMRs engage in head drumming 'duets' across territories, but the information encoded in these signals (dominance, sex, age, identity) is not well understood.
results.evaluation: Claim C23 is supported by citation (Rado et al., 1987), while C24 acknowledges the knowledge gap with supporting citations (Randall, 2013; Seyfarth and Cheney, 2003; Tibbetts and Dale, 2007). This identifies an important area for future research.

results.result: BMR courtship involves multimodal signaling (seismic, vocal, olfactory, tactile), copulatory pairs spend brief periods together before separating, and estrous females can discriminate and prefer homospecific male courtship calls.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C27 are supported by multiple citations (Gazit and Terkel, 2000; Nevo, 1961, 1969; Shanas et al., 1995; Nevo et al., 1987) describing reproductive behavior and mate choice mechanisms.

results.result: BMR gestation is 34 days producing 3-4 pups; mother-pup communication shifts from vocalizations to seismic signals during development; mothers show greater aggression toward male pups; dispersal begins at ~2 months and juveniles establish territories by ~3 months.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C33 are supported by multiple citations (Gazit et al., 1996; Rado et al., 1991b; Gazit and Terkel, 1998) describing reproductive biology and developmental transitions from social to solitary behavior.

results.result: BMRs integrate photoperiodic changes and entrain circadian rhythms through their atrophied eyes; in prairie voles, temperature and photoperiod alterations affect gonadotropin-releasing hormone synthesis and reproductive function.
results.evaluation: Claim C34 is supported by reference to another manuscript section with supporting evidence. Claim C35 is supported by citation (Kriegsfeld et al., 2001) and provides comparative context for understanding environmental regulation of reproduction.

results.result: BMRs are generalist foragers that cache food items (geophytes, herbaceous plants) essential for year-round survival, remaining largely inactive in deep, cool tunnels during summer.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C38 are supported by multiple citations (Galil, 1967; Heth, 1989; Lövy et al., 2015; Rado et al., 1993; Vleck, 1979) describing foraging ecology and seasonal activity patterns.

results.result: BMRs have superior spatial memory compared to rats, learning mazes significantly faster and retaining 45% performance after 120 days; their tunnels can extend up to 100m.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C40 are supported by citation (Kimchi and Terkel, 2001) demonstrating exceptional spatial memory. Claim C41 provides context about tunnel dimensions. These findings support the BMR's cognitive adaptations to subterranean navigation.

results.result: BMRs possess rudimentary eyes (<1mm diameter) covered by furred skin with degenerated lenses embedded in hypertrophied harderian glands; their retinas contain <900 ganglion cells (vs >50,000 in rats), and brain structures for image processing are severely regressed and dysfunctional.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C46 are supported by multiple citations (Cooper et al., 1993a,b; Haim et al., 1983; Rado et al., 1992; Gao et al., 2016) providing detailed anatomical evidence of visual system degeneration.

results.result: The dorsal lateral geniculate body (primary visual thalamic nucleus) in BMRs is strongly activated by auditory stimuli, demonstrating cross-modal neuroplasticity where visual processing areas have been repurposed for auditory processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C47 and C135 are supported by multiple citations (Bronchti et al., 2002, 1989; Heil et al., 1991) demonstrating remarkable brain plasticity. This represents a major finding of natural sensory compensation and neural reorganization.

results.result: Despite lacking short-wave opsin cones, BMR retinas contain three photoreceptor types (rhodopsin, coneopsin, L/M cone opsin) that enable light-induced gene expression in the SCN and entrainment of circadian locomotor rhythms; enucleation abolishes these light responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C52 are supported by multiple citations (David-Gray et al., 2002, 1999, 1998; Esquiva et al., 2016; Burda, 2006; Vuillez et al., 1994; Rado et al., 1991a; Pevet et al., 1984) demonstrating that despite blindness, BMRs retain functional non-image-forming photoreception for circadian regulation.

results.result: The BMR harderian gland synthesizes melatonin, is involved in photoperiodic detection, and contains melatonin receptors suggested to provide negative feedback control; the eusocial Damaraland mole-rat also shows photoperiod-modulated circadian melatonin rhythms.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C56 are supported by multiple citations (Balemans et al., 1980; Pevet et al., 1984; Gilad et al., 1997; Richter et al., 2006) describing the harderian gland's role in photoperiodic perception and melatonin regulation.

results.result: BMRs possess magnetoreception abilities used for nest and food cache placement; 180° magnetic field reversal causes corresponding shifts in preferred locations; experiments were conducted in darkness suggesting light-independent magnetoreception, though eye removal impairs magnetic sensing in Ansell's mole-rats.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C58 and C60 are supported by citations (Kimchi and Terkel, 2001) demonstrating magnetoreception in BMRs. However, there is conflicting evidence: C59 (Caspar et al., 2020) suggests eye-based receptors in related species, while C60-C61 suggest light-independent mechanisms. The location and mechanism of magnetoreceptors in BMRs remains unresolved, requiring further investigation.

results.result: Subterranean rodents (Highveld and Zambian mole rats) are more sensitive to low frequencies (0.8 kHz) with restricted hearing ranges compared to surface-dwelling rodents like house mice (peak sensitivity 16 kHz).
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C65 are supported by multiple citations (Dent et al., 2018; He et al., 2021; Müller and Burda, 1989; Brückmann and Burda, 1997; Heffner and Masterton, 1980) establishing the acoustic adaptations of subterranean vs. surface-dwelling rodents.

results.result: BMRs have reduced hearing sensitivity (peak 32 dB SPL at 1 kHz) compared to surface rodents (guinea pig: -9 dB SPL), hearing range 54 Hz-5.6 kHz at 60 dB SPL, poor sound localization abilities, and cannot localize signals <400ms duration (best at 1.2ms bursts).
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C72 are supported by multiple citations (Prosen et al., 1978; Heffner and Heffner, 1992, 1993) providing detailed audiometric data demonstrating BMR hearing limitations consistent with subterranean adaptations.

results.result: BMRs lack external pinnae and have uniquely structured middle and inner ears creating inefficient airborne sound transmission.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C74 are supported by citation (Rado et al., 1989) and Figure 2, describing morphological adaptations consistent with reduced airborne hearing sensitivity.

results.result: Giant mole rats have 14 call types determined by behavioral context and spectro-temporal features with peak frequencies <5 kHz; eusocial naked mole rats show colony-specific dialects in 'soft chirp' calls signifying group membership.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 are supported by citations (Bednářová et al., 2013; Barker et al., 2021b) providing comparative context for understanding vocal communication diversity among mole rat species.

results.result: BMRs have at least six call types (all <8 kHz) used for mother-pup communication and male courtship; courtship calls differ across chromosomal subspecies and play a role in assortative mating; distress calls have peak frequencies of 4-6 kHz.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C82 are supported by multiple citations (Capranica et al., 1974; Gazit and Terkel, 1998, 2000; Rado et al., 1991b; Nevo, 1969; Heth et al., 1988; Nevo et al., 1987; Bronchti et al., 1989) describing BMR vocal repertoire and its behavioral functions.

results.result: BMRs produce vibrational signals by head drumming on tunnel ceilings (2-4 drums/burst, 0.3s duration, 100-250 Hz, traveling ≥10m) and perceive these signals via jaw-to-tunnel bone conduction to the inner ear and via paw mechanoreceptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C86 are supported by multiple citations (Heth et al., 1987; Rado et al., 1987, 1989; Mason et al., 2010; Kimchi et al., 2005) and Figure 4, providing detailed description of vibrational communication production and perception mechanisms.

results.result: Vibration stimuli to the lower jaw evoke auditory brainstem responses in BMRs; bilaterally deafened BMRs lose vibration responses and cease head drumming within 4-6 weeks.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C88 are supported by citation (Rado et al., 1998) providing experimental evidence that vibrational signal perception depends on the auditory system via bone conduction.

results.result: The occipital cortex in BMRs is activated by both vibrational (100 Hz) and acoustic (2.5-4.4 kHz) frequencies, with two distinct cell clusters responding to frequencies matching long-distance vibratory signals and airborne social vocalizations.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C90 are supported by multiple citations (Bronchti et al., 2002; Heil et al., 1991; Sadka and Wollberg, 2004) demonstrating cortical processing of both vibrational and acoustic signals in visual cortex areas, further evidence of cross-modal plasticity.

results.result: The BMR somatosensory cortex extends into the occipital cortex and is 1.7 times larger than in laboratory rats when accounting for body weight and brain size differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C92 are supported by citations (Necker et al., 1992; Rehkämper et al., 1994; Mann et al., 1997) demonstrating expanded somatosensory representation consistent with heavy reliance on tactile information.

results.result: BMR rhinarium contains Merkel cell-axon complexes and Meissner's corpuscles; BMRs engage in 'wall seeking' behavior during maze tasks, perform better in narrow mazes allowing constant wall contact (opposite of rats), and naturally dig tunnels matching their body width for maximal tactile information.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C97 are supported by multiple citations (Klauer et al., 1997; Kimchi et al., 2004; Kimchi and Terkel, 2000, 2002) describing tactile specializations and their behavioral manifestations in navigation.

results.result: In naked mole rats, incisors are represented in approximately 31% of the somatosensory cortex.
results.evaluation: Claim C98 is supported by citations (Catania and Remple, 2002; Park et al., 2007) and provides comparative context suggesting BMRs may have similar incisor representation given their reliance on teeth for digging and aggression.

results.result: BMRs use seismic signaling for echolocation to detect obstacles in tunnels, adjusting bypass strategies based on obstacle size; echolocation head drums are higher frequency (250-300 Hz) single hits at ~8s intervals; modeling shows wavelengths are sufficient for detecting reflected waves at 30-50cm distance.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C103 are supported by multiple citations (Kimchi et al., 2005; Kimchi and Terkel, 2003a,b) and Figure 3C, providing experimental and modeling evidence for seismic echolocation behavior.

results.result: BMRs detect seismic signals via their paws, which contain 15-20 lamellated Pacinian corpuscles sensitive to 10-400 Hz vibrations.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C105 are supported by citations (Kimchi et al., 2005; McIntyre, 1980) identifying the mechanoreceptors responsible for paw-based vibration detection.

results.result: BMRs use olfaction to discriminate poisonous vs. edible food items from plant kairomones in soil and possess dorsoventrally flattened, wide snouts (~15mm in adults).
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C107 are supported by citations (Heth et al., 1992, 2002), personal observations, and Figure 2, describing olfactory foraging abilities and morphological adaptations.

results.result: The BMR VNO opens to the nasal cavity (not oral cavity) and shows an 8.5-fold postnatal length increase (1.5mm at 4 days to 13mm in adults), much greater than African mole rats (<1-fold increase) and naked mole rats (no volumetric growth).
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C111 are supported by multiple citations (Zuri et al., 1998a; Dennis et al., 2020; Smith et al., 2007) demonstrating substantial VNO development in BMRs compared to other mole rat species, suggesting enhanced pheromone detection capabilities.

results.result: There has been convergent reduction of V1R vomeronasal receptors in different subterranean rodents including BMRs.
results.evaluation: Claim C112 is supported by citations (Jiao et al., 2019; Zhao, 2021) indicating evolutionary reduction of airborne pheromone receptors, possibly due to limited airflow in underground tunnels.

results.result: BMRs secrete pheromones from the harderian gland via self-grooming; the gland is sexually dimorphic (larger in males) in size, weight, and chemical composition, correlates with body mass and season, and pheromone secretion during social interactions signals submissiveness and appeasement.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C116 are supported by multiple citations (Shanas and Terkel, 1995, 1999, 1997) describing harderian gland pheromone production and its role in social signaling.

results.result: Male BMRs use urine and feces for territorial scent marking; urinary pheromones are important for courtship and territoriality in both sexes; females are attracted to males with high urinary testosterone; lab-housed males have significantly lower androgens than wild males, possibly explaining low captive breeding success; estrous females prefer homospecific male odors.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C121 are supported by multiple citations (Gazit et al., 1997; Heth et al., 1992; Gottreich et al., 2000; Shanas et al., 1995; Nevo et al., 1976) describing the complex role of olfactory signals in territorial and reproductive behaviors.

results.result: In eusocial naked mole rats and Ansell's mole rats, most oxytocin cells are in the PVN and SON; no sexual dimorphism in OT neuron number was found in prairie voles, Ansell's mole rats, or naked mole rats.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C125 are supported by multiple citations (Rosen et al., 2008; Valesky et al., 2012; Yamamoto et al., 2004; Mooney and Holmes, 2013) providing comparative neuroanatomical data on oxytocin systems across rodent species.

results.result: BMR PVN contains significantly lower numbers of OT neurons compared to mice (accounting for brain size differences), with no sex differences in OT cell numbers.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C127 are based on preliminary unpublished data from the authors' laboratory. While the findings are plausible and consistent with the BMR's solitary phenotype, they cannot be fully evaluated without peer-reviewed publication including methodological details, sample sizes, and statistical analyses.

results.result: In naked mole rats, subordinate individuals have more PVN OT neurons than breeding individuals; peripheral OT administration enhances social behaviors (huddling, proximity, investigations) blocked by OT antagonist; no OT/AVP differences were found across social ranks in Ansell's mole rats.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C130 are supported by citations (Mooney and Holmes, 2013; Mooney et al., 2014; Valesky et al., 2012) demonstrating species-specific relationships between oxytocin systems and social behavior in mole rats.

results.result: Shank3b KO mice (ASD model) have reduced PVN OT neuron numbers.
results.evaluation: Claim C131 is supported by citation (Resendez et al., 2020) and provides translational context linking oxytocin deficits to autism-like social behavior deficits.

results.result: Early life stress effects on aggression and AVP expression vary by species: enhanced aggression with AVP upregulation in male rats vs. decreased aggression with AVP downregulation in mice and mandarin voles.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C133 are supported by multiple citations (Veenema et al., 2006; Veenema and Neumann, 2009; Tsuda et al., 2011; Wei et al., 2013) demonstrating species-specific relationships between vasopressin and aggression.

results.result: Considerable differences in CRF abundance and receptor binding in the telencephalon exist between eusocial naked mole rats and solitary Cape mole rats.
results.evaluation: Claim C134 is supported by citation (Coen et al., 2015) suggesting CRF system differences may relate to social strategy differences between mole rat species.

results.result: There is no known method to determine the age of adult BMRs captured in the field.
results.evaluation: Claim C136 is stated as a limitation in BMR research and represents an important methodological constraint for field studies.

results.result: A Spalax ehrenbergi genome assembly exists for one female BMR; transcriptomic analyses have revealed differential expression under underground stress conditions; scRNA sequencing of microglia shows similarities to other rodents.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C139 are supported by citations (Fang et al., 2014; Malik et al., 2011; Geirsdottir et al., 2019) documenting available genomic and transcriptomic resources for BMR research.

results.result: Successful transformation of naked mole rat cells has been achieved using a novel CRISPR gRNA library and lentiviral vectors.
results.evaluation: Claim C140 is supported by citations (Hadi, 2020a; Hadi et al., 2020b) representing a methodological advance that may enable genetic manipulation in mole rats including BMRs.
